articles.title: How AI is De-Risking Drug Development and Companion Diagnostics
articles.text:
Skip to main content Opinion How AI is De-Risking Drug Development and Companion Diagnostics Digital pathology and artificial intelligence are transforming the drug development landscape, accelerating the path to personalized medicine and better health outcomes. Written by Karan Arora Karan Arora Karan Arora is the Senior Vice President of Advanced Assays, AI, and Pharma Services at Leica Biosystems. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . and Luiza Moore, MD, PhD Luiza Moore, MD, PhD Luiza Moore, MD, PhD, FRCPath is the Global Commercial Product Leader – AI Enabled Assays, at Leica Biosystems. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 12, 2026 | 7 min read Save for Later Companion diagnostics enable more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Image credit: © iStock.com, Yuuji PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Share T he path to bringing a new drug to market is increasingly complex and costly, with development costs now exceeding $2 billion and timelines approaching a decade. 1,2 The stakes have never been higher—demanding new models, new technologies, and new thinking to reduce risk and accelerate breakthroughs. Up to 90 percent of compounds entering clinical trials never reach the market, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy in heterogenous patient populations. This high failure rate has accelerated a shift toward more targeted development strategies. Companion diagnostics are central to this shift, enabling more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape—not only for therapeutics but also for precision diagnostics that guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Digital pathology and AI now sit at the heart of this transformation, offering new ways to extract quantitative biological signals, harmonize global lab variability, and support earlier, sharper decision‑making in clinical trials. 3 From Failure to Focus: Reducing Drug Development Risk with Computational Pathology Biology is heterogeneous, traditional pathology is variable, and global clinical trial operations introduce noise that can obscure early efficacy or safety signals. 4 Whole‑slide imaging (WSI) and computational pathology have the potential to directly address these challenges by scaling objective readouts from tissue and associated morphology with clinical outcomes. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe With over 15 years of experience in diagnostics and pathology, I have seen how “identical” hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) slides can vary across sites—introducing noise, repeat reviews, and delayed decisions. This becomes particularly challenging when variability forces the tissue journey to restart, or worse, necessitates repeat tissue collection from patients, many of whom are critically ill—consuming precious, often irreplaceable patient samples and driving additional trial costs. AI‑enabled tissue quantification has the potential to address these challenges by reducing subjectivity, delivering more reproducible endpoints, and generating cleaner data earlier in drug development. AI can also serve as a second set of eyes during review, helping ensure critical features are not missed and increasing confidence in study outcomes. From Slides to Quantitative Biomarkers Modern AI models are capable of identifying subtle morphologic patterns that correlate with prognosis, molecular status, and treatment response. For example, multiple‑instance learning (MIL)-based approaches have matured to clinical‑grade performance for predicting histology-derived endpoints, providing objective, reproducible metrics appropriate for global deployment and regulatory evaluation. 5 These biomarkers further reduce biological uncertainty by enabling earlier biological signal detection and quantitative features that can be deployed consistently across global trials. This shift allows development teams to detect trends long before traditional clinical endpoints mature. 6 Strengthening Oncology Trial Decisions Through Early AI‑Enabled Signal Detection AI‑enabled biomarkers support early patient stratification, reduce biological and operational noise, and enable more accurate response prediction across oncology trials . Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6 This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6 Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7 Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8 Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions. Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery. Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness. In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support. Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development. In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines. Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment. AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10 As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment. AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate. The Future: Multimodal, Generalizable, and Equitable Next‑generation multimodal foundation models integrate histology with clinical reports, genomics, and proteomics to improve disease classification, survival prediction, and biological interpretability across cancer types. These models move beyond single‑modality analysis, enabling richer context and more biologically meaningful insights. 8 When rigorously validated across sites and paired with stain‑robust deployment‑ready pipelines, these systems have the potential to expand access to precision diagnostics globally, including in low‑resource settings where specialist expertise and advanced infrastructure may be limited. 3,11 Importantly, AI is not a substitute for skilled laboratory staff and researchers; rather it serves as a powerful second set of eyes—enhancing precision, increasing agility, and elevating the quality of scientific work with deeper insights. Collaboration Delivers Greater Value In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed. Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed. Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact. Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact. As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics. Profile The Cancer Epidemiologist Who Championed HPV Vaccines to End Cervical Cancer Anna Giuliano’s research on HPV infections and vaccines helped transform cervical cancer from a leading killer into a disease that the WHO now believes can be eliminated. Written by Sneha Khedkar Sneha Khedkar Go to The Scientist's LinkedIn Page Sneha Khedkar is an Assistant Editor at The Scientist . She has a Master's degree in biochemistry and has written for Scientific American , New Scientist , and Knowable Magazine , among others. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jan 20, 2026 | 8 min read Save for Later Anna Giuliano, a cancer epidemiologist at the Moffitt Cancer Center, studies the epidemiology of HPV and approaches to protect people from HPV-associated cancers. Giuliano is photographed here at the Cancer Moonshot meeting at the White House. Image credit: Anna Giuliano PDF version Share A s a child in Manhattan, Anna Giuliano , a cancer epidemiologist at the Moffitt Cancer Center, experienced a cultural melting pot. Born to a Colombian mother and first-generation American father, she knew people whose families, like hers, had roots in other countries. “I grew up in a very multicultural environment in the city and that was always something that I loved and I very much enjoyed,” said Giuliano. This motivated her to pursue a career that would help people from diverse backgrounds. In the 1980s, after her graduate studies, she got her wish: a chance to study the human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes cervical cancer. “It turns out that cervical cancer has so many of the elements that I found interesting,” said Giuliano. “It continues to be and it definitely was in the 1980s a cancer of women…who are of lower socioeconomic status. It's multicultural.” Giuliano’s work has contributed to a better understanding of HPV-associated diseases in both women and men. Moffitt Cancer Center Over the next few decades, Giuliano studied the role of HPV in cancers in both women and men. 1,2 She also played a central role in the clinical testing of HPV vaccinations to prevent cancers linked to the virus. 3 She has led a number of cancer epidemiology studies and clinical trials among diverse populations in several parts of the world, contributing to a better understanding of the virus’s role in diseases in both women and men. Her work proved crucial in shaping HPV-linked cancer elimination statements and ensuing guidelines to achieve this from National Cancer Institute centers and the World Health Organization (WHO). Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Trading the Violin Bow for a Pipette Despite her extensive experience in cervical cancer research, Giuliano’s original career trajectory was completely unrelated. “My first goal in life was to be a concert violinist,” she recalled. However, as she attended the High School of Music & Art in New York, she realized she may not be able to achieve this dream—but another door opened. “You’ll see this [in people who play] string instruments and piano. A lot of us tend to gravitate towards the math and sciences,” noted Giuliano. During her graduate studies at Tufts University, Giuliano became interested in pathology. When she expressed her enthusiasm in the field to Martha Hutchinson , who headed the pathology department at Tufts University at that time, Hutchinson offered her a piece of advice that shaped Giuliano’s career path. “[Hutchinson] said, ‘This group from Germany has identified this virus that they think is the cause of cervical cancer. So, I want you to learn everything that you can about it’,” recalled Giuliano. This virus was HPV, which virologist Harald zur Hausen and his colleagues had found in cervical cancer samples. Scientists also found that DNA from HPV-16, the HPV type most commonly found in cervical cancer cells, could induce cancer-like traits in cultured cells, validating that HPV infections could cause cervical cancer. 4 Given this compelling evidence and Hutchinson’s nudge, Giuliano knew what she wanted to do after finishing her graduate studies in 1989. “I'm going to prevent cervical cancer,” Giuliano declared back then. She chose to pursue a fellowship at the University of Arizona, where she could be close to the US-Mexico border, an area that had one of the highest rates of cervical cancer. 5 Chasing a Better Understanding of HPV Infections and Cancers At the University of Arizona, Giuliano crossed paths with gynecological oncologists Kenneth Hatch and Achim Schneider . Hatch was interested in learning more about nutrition in cervical cancer, and Schneider had trained under zur Hausen, who eventually went on to win the Nobel Prize for his discovery that HPV causes cervical cancer. A common goal united Giuliano, Hatch, and Schneider: They wanted to better understand HPV infections and cervical cancer . “It was a trifecta,” recalled Giuliano. “It was Ken as a physician, Achim, who set up the first HPV assays, and me as a burgeoning epidemiologist.” However, the trio had to fight through meager funding, which was difficult to come by since cervical cancer incidence was low in the US. “We spent a lot of time writing grants and then revising and resubmitting and so on,” said Giuliano. “A lot of that time could have just been done spent working on the research.” Despite this, they persevered and uncovered important insights about HPV infections and cervical cancer. One of their first findings was that people with recurrent HPV infections had lower antioxidant nutrients levels in their plasma. This helped establish that nutrient cofactors played a role in HPV infection risk. 6 Beyond nutritional studies, Giuliano and her team’s epidemiological studies helped elucidate the rate at which HPV infections are acquired and cleared. 7 Over time, she went on to investigate HPV in multicultural populations, realizing her dream of helping people from diverse backgrounds. At the turn of the century, scientists recognized that people from minority populations were at risk of acquiring HPV infections due to poor diet, early age of first intercourse, and multiple sexual partners. 8 However, few epidemiological studies included minority populations in the US, impeding scientists from getting a complete picture of HPV incidence among people from these backgrounds. 9 Giuliano and her team recruited participants belonging to Black and Hispanic populations and found that they had a higher HPV infection burden compared to people from majority populations. This offered significant evidence that certain groups would benefit more from vaccination efforts. 8,10 HPV Vaccine Testing in Women and Men In 1999, Giuliano received a phone call that proved to be pivotal. Eliav Barr , who was leading the clinical development program for the HPV vaccine at Merck, contacted Giuliano seeking a collaboration. He had come across one of her research abstracts and hoped her expertise would help him and his team conduct vaccine trials in healthy volunteers and follow them up over a long duration. “I said, ‘Yeah this is wonderful. I'm so excited to be part of the program’,” Giuliano recalled. The duo initially tested a monovalent vaccine—against one HPV antigen—followed by studies involving multivalent vaccines. 11,12 This culminated in a broad-spectrum FDA-approved vaccine that protects against nine HPV strains that cause nearly 90 percent of all cervical cancers. 13 As the president of the International Papillomavirus Society (IPVS), Giuliano presided over the final comments at the IPVS 2025 conference held in Bangkok. Anna Giuliano However, vaccinating women solved only half the problem. Studies in men revealed that they exhibited a higher prevalence of HPV infections compared to women. 14 Through her own research, Guiliano also had a good understanding of the natural history of HPV infection and screening strategies in men. 15 Since men could transmit HPV to their female sexual partners to potentially cause cervical cancer, Giuliano championed for the need to vaccinate men to protect both sexes against the virus. 16 So, over time, Giuliano and Barr expanded their studies to include men and found that a multivalent vaccine protected them from HPV infection and its associated complications. 17 Giuliano believes that her work on understanding HPV mechanism and investigating HPV vaccine efficacy in men has been her most impactful and significant contribution to the field. Noel Brewer , a public health researcher at the University of North Carolina, who has met Giuliano at several conferences, agreed. “She's made really important contributions to our understanding of HPV in men,” he said. “She helped to move the US and other countries to approve the vaccine for men by establishing the epidemiology of HPV and associated disease in men and the impact of HPV vaccination on men's health.” Setting Sights on Eliminating Cervical Cancer When she moved to the Moffitt Cancer Center in 2004, Giuliano continued pursuing investigations related to cancer epidemiology among diverse populations. Her work offered a better understanding of HPV infections’ natural history, which expanded on the foundation laid by Pap smears for cervical screening. 18 For instance, she helped measure the burden of HPV infections in cancers other than that of the cervix to quantify the rate at which infection occurred and got cleared. 19,20 Parallelly, she continued working on improving HPV vaccinations and advocating the need to make the vaccines available. “[Giuliano] is one of the leading figures who developed the argument that cervical cancer could be eliminated,” noted Brewer. She championed for the elimination of HPV-related cancers and argued that this was feasible in countries that have resources for immunizations, screenings, and pre-cancer treatments. She also acted as a consultant to the WHO regarding HPV vaccination and research on cervical cancer. “[Giuliano’s] powerful framing of the epidemiological data led the WHO to establish a global initiative to eliminate cervical cancer.” Brewer noted that this helped increase the global reach of HPV vaccinations from 40 percent to roughly 90 percent of at-risk populations. “This will save millions of lives,” he added. In fact, Giuliano’s work continues to strengthen the three main pillars which are the basis of WHO’s target for eliminating cervical cancer: HPV vaccination, cervical screening, and precancer and cancer treatment. 18 HPV vaccine uptake significantly increased among both female and male populations in the US. Designed by Erin Lemieux; data adapted from World Health Organization Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination coverage . In part due to her efforts, along with those of others in the field, the rate of cervical cancer cases has dropped from 9.3 new cases per 100,000 people in 1990 to 7.8 new cases per 100,000 people in 2021 globally . The incidence also reduced in the US from 10.2 new cases per 100,000 people in 1990 to 6.5 new cases per 100,000 people in 2021. Maintaining a Legacy: Shaping Policies and Young Minds Over time, Giuliano’s drive became a lesson for those she mentored. Brittney Dickey , who joined Giuliano’s group as a postdoctoral researcher in 2020, recalled how Giuliano advised her to define her career by a long-term goal. Giuliano’s research extends to countries outside of the US. She participated in a three-day HPV workshop in Harare, Zimbabwe, focused on the basic science of HPV and associated diseases, and methods for their prevention, early detection, and treatment. Participants included people from Zimbabwe, Botswana, South Africa, and Zambia Anna Giuliano Towards the end of her postdoctoral fellowship, Dickey confided in Giuliano about her lack of motivation at the time. “She said, ‘You have to figure out what your passion is’,” recalled Dickey, now a public health researcher at University of Nebraska Medical Center. “And if you have that goal and you have something that you're working towards every day, it helps motivate you in those small projects.” Dickey observed this first-hand about Giuliano. “At some point along the way, she realized her passion was to eliminate HPV. It's very evident that that drives her as a scientist,” said Dickey. Indeed, Giuliano persisted against all odds and went on to work toward her dream, laying the foundation for efforts—including better screening and vaccinations—aimed at eliminating cervical cancer. Reflecting on her career, Giuliano said that one of the most exciting aspects has been seeing how well the vaccine works. “It is incredibly rare as a cancer researcher to develop a…product that has such great efficacy across the board across all males, females, different ages, different ethnicities, different world regions,” she said. “It's just been phenomenal. It's so hard to explain how wonderful that is.” Despite the success, she acknowledged that the problem is not completely solved yet. According to her, scientists, investors, governments, and other stakeholders must come together to develop sustainable programs for global dissemination of the vaccine. She hopes that in this manner, all people who are eligible receive the vaccine. “That would be my dream.” References Ferris DG, et al. Written by Karan Arora Karan Arora Karan Arora is the Senior Vice President of Advanced Assays, AI, and Pharma Services at Leica Biosystems. Image credit: © iStock.com, Yuuji PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Share T he path to bringing a new drug to market is increasingly complex and costly, with development costs now exceeding $2 billion and timelines approaching a decade. 1,2 The stakes have never been higher—demanding new models, new technologies, and new thinking to reduce risk and accelerate breakthroughs. Up to 90 percent of compounds entering clinical trials never reach the market, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy in heterogenous patient populations. This high failure rate has accelerated a shift toward more targeted development strategies. Companion diagnostics are central to this shift, enabling more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape—not only for therapeutics but also for precision diagnostics that guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Digital pathology and AI now sit at the heart of this transformation, offering new ways to extract quantitative biological signals, harmonize global lab variability, and support earlier, sharper decision‑making in clinical trials. 3 From Failure to Focus: Reducing Drug Development Risk with Computational Pathology Biology is heterogeneous, traditional pathology is variable, and global clinical trial operations introduce noise that can obscure early efficacy or safety signals. 4 Whole‑slide imaging (WSI) and computational pathology have the potential to directly address these challenges by scaling objective readouts from tissue and associated morphology with clinical outcomes. Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe With over 15 years of experience in diagnostics and pathology, I have seen how “identical” hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) slides can vary across sites—introducing noise, repeat reviews, and delayed decisions. This becomes particularly challenging when variability forces the tissue journey to restart, or worse, necessitates repeat tissue collection from patients, many of whom are critically ill—consuming precious, often irreplaceable patient samples and driving additional trial costs. AI‑enabled tissue quantification has the potential to address these challenges by reducing subjectivity, delivering more reproducible endpoints, and generating cleaner data earlier in drug development. AI can also serve as a second set of eyes during review, helping ensure critical features are not missed and increasing confidence in study outcomes. From Slides to Quantitative Biomarkers Modern AI models are capable of identifying subtle morphologic patterns that correlate with prognosis, molecular status, and treatment response. For example, multiple‑instance learning (MIL)-based approaches have matured to clinical‑grade performance for predicting histology-derived endpoints, providing objective, reproducible metrics appropriate for global deployment and regulatory evaluation. 5 These biomarkers further reduce biological uncertainty by enabling earlier biological signal detection and quantitative features that can be deployed consistently across global trials. This shift allows development teams to detect trends long before traditional clinical endpoints mature. 6 Strengthening Oncology Trial Decisions Through Early AI‑Enabled Signal Detection AI‑enabled biomarkers support early patient stratification, reduce biological and operational noise, and enable more accurate response prediction across oncology trials . Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6 This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6 Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7 Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8 Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions. Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery. Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness. In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support. Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development. In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines. Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment. AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10 As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment. AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate. The Future: Multimodal, Generalizable, and Equitable Next‑generation multimodal foundation models integrate histology with clinical reports, genomics, and proteomics to improve disease classification, survival prediction, and biological interpretability across cancer types. These models move beyond single‑modality analysis, enabling richer context and more biologically meaningful insights. 8 When rigorously validated across sites and paired with stain‑robust deployment‑ready pipelines, these systems have the potential to expand access to precision diagnostics globally, including in low‑resource settings where specialist expertise and advanced infrastructure may be limited. 3,11 Importantly, AI is not a substitute for skilled laboratory staff and researchers; rather it serves as a powerful second set of eyes—enhancing precision, increasing agility, and elevating the quality of scientific work with deeper insights. Collaboration Delivers Greater Value In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed. Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed. Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact. Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact. As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics. Jan 20, 2026 | 8 min read Save for Later Anna Giuliano, a cancer epidemiologist at the Moffitt Cancer Center, studies the epidemiology of HPV and approaches to protect people from HPV-associated cancers. Giuliano is photographed here at the Cancer Moonshot meeting at the White House. Image credit: Anna Giuliano PDF version Share A s a child in Manhattan, Anna Giuliano , a cancer epidemiologist at the Moffitt Cancer Center, experienced a cultural melting pot. Born to a Colombian mother and first-generation American father, she knew people whose families, like hers, had roots in other countries. “I grew up in a very multicultural environment in the city and that was always something that I loved and I very much enjoyed,” said Giuliano. This motivated her to pursue a career that would help people from diverse backgrounds. In the 1980s, after her graduate studies, she got her wish: a chance to study the human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes cervical cancer. “It turns out that cervical cancer has so many of the elements that I found interesting,” said Giuliano. “It continues to be and it definitely was in the 1980s a cancer of women…who are of lower socioeconomic status. It's multicultural.” Giuliano’s work has contributed to a better understanding of HPV-associated diseases in both women and men. Moffitt Cancer Center Over the next few decades, Giuliano studied the role of HPV in cancers in both women and men. 1,2 She also played a central role in the clinical testing of HPV vaccinations to prevent cancers linked to the virus. 3 She has led a number of cancer epidemiology studies and clinical trials among diverse populations in several parts of the world, contributing to a better understanding of the virus’s role in diseases in both women and men. Her work proved crucial in shaping HPV-linked cancer elimination statements and ensuing guidelines to achieve this from National Cancer Institute centers and the World Health Organization (WHO). Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Trading the Violin Bow for a Pipette Despite her extensive experience in cervical cancer research, Giuliano’s original career trajectory was completely unrelated. “My first goal in life was to be a concert violinist,” she recalled. However, as she attended the High School of Music & Art in New York, she realized she may not be able to achieve this dream—but another door opened. “You’ll see this [in people who play] string instruments and piano. A lot of us tend to gravitate towards the math and sciences,” noted Giuliano. During her graduate studies at Tufts University, Giuliano became interested in pathology. When she expressed her enthusiasm in the field to Martha Hutchinson , who headed the pathology department at Tufts University at that time, Hutchinson offered her a piece of advice that shaped Giuliano’s career path. “[Hutchinson] said, ‘This group from Germany has identified this virus that they think is the cause of cervical cancer. So, I want you to learn everything that you can about it’,” recalled Giuliano. This virus was HPV, which virologist Harald zur Hausen and his colleagues had found in cervical cancer samples. Scientists also found that DNA from HPV-16, the HPV type most commonly found in cervical cancer cells, could induce cancer-like traits in cultured cells, validating that HPV infections could cause cervical cancer. 4 Given this compelling evidence and Hutchinson’s nudge, Giuliano knew what she wanted to do after finishing her graduate studies in 1989. “I'm going to prevent cervical cancer,” Giuliano declared back then. She chose to pursue a fellowship at the University of Arizona, where she could be close to the US-Mexico border, an area that had one of the highest rates of cervical cancer. 5 Chasing a Better Understanding of HPV Infections and Cancers At the University of Arizona, Giuliano crossed paths with gynecological oncologists Kenneth Hatch and Achim Schneider . Hatch was interested in learning more about nutrition in cervical cancer, and Schneider had trained under zur Hausen, who eventually went on to win the Nobel Prize for his discovery that HPV causes cervical cancer. A common goal united Giuliano, Hatch, and Schneider: They wanted to better understand HPV infections and cervical cancer . “It was a trifecta,” recalled Giuliano. “It was Ken as a physician, Achim, who set up the first HPV assays, and me as a burgeoning epidemiologist.” However, the trio had to fight through meager funding, which was difficult to come by since cervical cancer incidence was low in the US. “We spent a lot of time writing grants and then revising and resubmitting and so on,” said Giuliano. “A lot of that time could have just been done spent working on the research.” Despite this, they persevered and uncovered important insights about HPV infections and cervical cancer. One of their first findings was that people with recurrent HPV infections had lower antioxidant nutrients levels in their plasma. This helped establish that nutrient cofactors played a role in HPV infection risk. 6 Beyond nutritional studies, Giuliano and her team’s epidemiological studies helped elucidate the rate at which HPV infections are acquired and cleared. 7 Over time, she went on to investigate HPV in multicultural populations, realizing her dream of helping people from diverse backgrounds. At the turn of the century, scientists recognized that people from minority populations were at risk of acquiring HPV infections due to poor diet, early age of first intercourse, and multiple sexual partners. 8 However, few epidemiological studies included minority populations in the US, impeding scientists from getting a complete picture of HPV incidence among people from these backgrounds. 9 Giuliano and her team recruited participants belonging to Black and Hispanic populations and found that they had a higher HPV infection burden compared to people from majority populations. This offered significant evidence that certain groups would benefit more from vaccination efforts. 8,10 HPV Vaccine Testing in Women and Men In 1999, Giuliano received a phone call that proved to be pivotal. Eliav Barr , who was leading the clinical development program for the HPV vaccine at Merck, contacted Giuliano seeking a collaboration. He had come across one of her research abstracts and hoped her expertise would help him and his team conduct vaccine trials in healthy volunteers and follow them up over a long duration. “I said, ‘Yeah this is wonderful. I'm so excited to be part of the program’,” Giuliano recalled. The duo initially tested a monovalent vaccine—against one HPV antigen—followed by studies involving multivalent vaccines. 11,12 This culminated in a broad-spectrum FDA-approved vaccine that protects against nine HPV strains that cause nearly 90 percent of all cervical cancers. 13 As the president of the International Papillomavirus Society (IPVS), Giuliano presided over the final comments at the IPVS 2025 conference held in Bangkok. Anna Giuliano However, vaccinating women solved only half the problem. Studies in men revealed that they exhibited a higher prevalence of HPV infections compared to women. 14 Through her own research, Guiliano also had a good understanding of the natural history of HPV infection and screening strategies in men. 15 Since men could transmit HPV to their female sexual partners to potentially cause cervical cancer, Giuliano championed for the need to vaccinate men to protect both sexes against the virus. 16 So, over time, Giuliano and Barr expanded their studies to include men and found that a multivalent vaccine protected them from HPV infection and its associated complications. 17 Giuliano believes that her work on understanding HPV mechanism and investigating HPV vaccine efficacy in men has been her most impactful and significant contribution to the field. Noel Brewer , a public health researcher at the University of North Carolina, who has met Giuliano at several conferences, agreed. “She's made really important contributions to our understanding of HPV in men,” he said. “She helped to move the US and other countries to approve the vaccine for men by establishing the epidemiology of HPV and associated disease in men and the impact of HPV vaccination on men's health.” Setting Sights on Eliminating Cervical Cancer When she moved to the Moffitt Cancer Center in 2004, Giuliano continued pursuing investigations related to cancer epidemiology among diverse populations. Her work offered a better understanding of HPV infections’ natural history, which expanded on the foundation laid by Pap smears for cervical screening. 18 For instance, she helped measure the burden of HPV infections in cancers other than that of the cervix to quantify the rate at which infection occurred and got cleared. 19,20 Parallelly, she continued working on improving HPV vaccinations and advocating the need to make the vaccines available. “[Giuliano] is one of the leading figures who developed the argument that cervical cancer could be eliminated,” noted Brewer. She championed for the elimination of HPV-related cancers and argued that this was feasible in countries that have resources for immunizations, screenings, and pre-cancer treatments. She also acted as a consultant to the WHO regarding HPV vaccination and research on cervical cancer. “[Giuliano’s] powerful framing of the epidemiological data led the WHO to establish a global initiative to eliminate cervical cancer.” Brewer noted that this helped increase the global reach of HPV vaccinations from 40 percent to roughly 90 percent of at-risk populations. “This will save millions of lives,” he added. In fact, Giuliano’s work continues to strengthen the three main pillars which are the basis of WHO’s target for eliminating cervical cancer: HPV vaccination, cervical screening, and precancer and cancer treatment. 18 HPV vaccine uptake significantly increased among both female and male populations in the US. In part due to her efforts, along with those of others in the field, the rate of cervical cancer cases has dropped from 9.3 new cases per 100,000 people in 1990 to 7.8 new cases per 100,000 people in 2021 globally . The incidence also reduced in the US from 10.2 new cases per 100,000 people in 1990 to 6.5 new cases per 100,000 people in 2021. Maintaining a Legacy: Shaping Policies and Young Minds Over time, Giuliano’s drive became a lesson for those she mentored. Brittney Dickey , who joined Giuliano’s group as a postdoctoral researcher in 2020, recalled how Giuliano advised her to define her career by a long-term goal. Giuliano’s research extends to countries outside of the US. She participated in a three-day HPV workshop in Harare, Zimbabwe, focused on the basic science of HPV and associated diseases, and methods for their prevention, early detection, and treatment. Participants included people from Zimbabwe, Botswana, South Africa, and Zambia Anna Giuliano Towards the end of her postdoctoral fellowship, Dickey confided in Giuliano about her lack of motivation at the time. “She said, ‘You have to figure out what your passion is’,” recalled Dickey, now a public health researcher at University of Nebraska Medical Center. “And if you have that goal and you have something that you're working towards every day, it helps motivate you in those small projects.” Dickey observed this first-hand about Giuliano. “At some point along the way, she realized her passion was to eliminate HPV. It's very evident that that drives her as a scientist,” said Dickey. Indeed, Giuliano persisted against all odds and went on to work toward her dream, laying the foundation for efforts—including better screening and vaccinations—aimed at eliminating cervical cancer. Reflecting on her career, Giuliano said that one of the most exciting aspects has been seeing how well the vaccine works. “It is incredibly rare as a cancer researcher to develop a…product that has such great efficacy across the board across all males, females, different ages, different ethnicities, different world regions,” she said. “It's just been phenomenal. It's so hard to explain how wonderful that is.” Despite the success, she acknowledged that the problem is not completely solved yet. According to her, scientists, investors, governments, and other stakeholders must come together to develop sustainable programs for global dissemination of the vaccine. She hopes that in this manner, all people who are eligible receive the vaccine. “That would be my dream.” References Ferris DG, et al. T he path to bringing a new drug to market is increasingly complex and costly, with development costs now exceeding $2 billion and timelines approaching a decade. 1,2 The stakes have never been higher—demanding new models, new technologies, and new thinking to reduce risk and accelerate breakthroughs. Up to 90 percent of compounds entering clinical trials never reach the market, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy in heterogenous patient populations. This high failure rate has accelerated a shift toward more targeted development strategies.
T
1,2
Companion diagnostics are central to this shift, enabling more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape—not only for therapeutics but also for precision diagnostics that guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Digital pathology and AI now sit at the heart of this transformation, offering new ways to extract quantitative biological signals, harmonize global lab variability, and support earlier, sharper decision‑making in clinical trials. 3
3
From Failure to Focus: Reducing Drug Development Risk with Computational Pathology
Biology is heterogeneous, traditional pathology is variable, and global clinical trial operations introduce noise that can obscure early efficacy or safety signals. 4 Whole‑slide imaging (WSI) and computational pathology have the potential to directly address these challenges by scaling objective readouts from tissue and associated morphology with clinical outcomes.

With over 15 years of experience in diagnostics and pathology, I have seen how “identical” hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) slides can vary across sites—introducing noise, repeat reviews, and delayed decisions. This becomes particularly challenging when variability forces the tissue journey to restart, or worse, necessitates repeat tissue collection from patients, many of whom are critically ill—consuming precious, often irreplaceable patient samples and driving additional trial costs.
AI‑enabled tissue quantification has the potential to address these challenges by reducing subjectivity, delivering more reproducible endpoints, and generating cleaner data earlier in drug development. AI can also serve as a second set of eyes during review, helping ensure critical features are not missed and increasing confidence in study outcomes.
From Slides to Quantitative Biomarkers
Modern AI models are capable of identifying subtle morphologic patterns that correlate with prognosis, molecular status, and treatment response. For example, multiple‑instance learning (MIL)-based approaches have matured to clinical‑grade performance for predicting histology-derived endpoints, providing objective, reproducible metrics appropriate for global deployment and regulatory evaluation. 5
Modern AI models
5
These biomarkers further reduce biological uncertainty by enabling earlier biological signal detection and quantitative features that can be deployed consistently across global trials. This shift allows development teams to detect trends long before traditional clinical endpoints mature. 6
6
Strengthening Oncology Trial Decisions Through Early AI‑Enabled Signal Detection
AI‑enabled biomarkers support early patient stratification, reduce biological and operational noise, and enable more accurate response prediction across oncology trials . Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6
oncology trials
This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6
3,6
Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development
Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7
7
Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines.
These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8
8
Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready
Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions.
Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery.
Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness.
In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support.
Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape
In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development.
CDx co‑development pathways
In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines.
European Medicines Agency
Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment.
AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows
AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10
9,10
As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment.
AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate.
The Future: Multimodal, Generalizable, and Equitable
Next‑generation multimodal foundation models integrate histology with clinical reports, genomics, and proteomics to improve disease classification, survival prediction, and biological interpretability across cancer types. These models move beyond single‑modality analysis, enabling richer context and more biologically meaningful insights. 8
When rigorously validated across sites and paired with stain‑robust deployment‑ready pipelines, these systems have the potential to expand access to precision diagnostics globally, including in low‑resource settings where specialist expertise and advanced infrastructure may be limited. 3,11
3,11
Importantly, AI is not a substitute for skilled laboratory staff and researchers; rather it serves as a powerful second set of eyes—enhancing precision, increasing agility, and elevating the quality of scientific work with deeper insights.
Collaboration Delivers Greater Value
In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed.
Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed.
Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation
As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact.
Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact.
As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics.

Profile The Cancer Epidemiologist Who Championed HPV Vaccines to End Cervical Cancer Anna Giuliano’s research on HPV infections and vaccines helped transform cervical cancer from a leading killer into a disease that the WHO now believes can be eliminated. Jan 20, 2026 | 8 min read Save for Later Anna Giuliano, a cancer epidemiologist at the Moffitt Cancer Center, studies the epidemiology of HPV and approaches to protect people from HPV-associated cancers. Giuliano is photographed here at the Cancer Moonshot meeting at the White House. Image credit: Anna Giuliano PDF version Share A s a child in Manhattan, Anna Giuliano , a cancer epidemiologist at the Moffitt Cancer Center, experienced a cultural melting pot. Born to a Colombian mother and first-generation American father, she knew people whose families, like hers, had roots in other countries. “I grew up in a very multicultural environment in the city and that was always something that I loved and I very much enjoyed,” said Giuliano. This motivated her to pursue a career that would help people from diverse backgrounds. In the 1980s, after her graduate studies, she got her wish: a chance to study the human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes cervical cancer. “It turns out that cervical cancer has so many of the elements that I found interesting,” said Giuliano. “It continues to be and it definitely was in the 1980s a cancer of women…who are of lower socioeconomic status. It's multicultural.” Giuliano’s work has contributed to a better understanding of HPV-associated diseases in both women and men. Moffitt Cancer Center Over the next few decades, Giuliano studied the role of HPV in cancers in both women and men. 1,2 She also played a central role in the clinical testing of HPV vaccinations to prevent cancers linked to the virus. 3 She has led a number of cancer epidemiology studies and clinical trials among diverse populations in several parts of the world, contributing to a better understanding of the virus’s role in diseases in both women and men. Her work proved crucial in shaping HPV-linked cancer elimination statements and ensuing guidelines to achieve this from National Cancer Institute centers and the World Health Organization (WHO). However, as she attended the High School of Music & Art in New York, she realized she may not be able to achieve this dream—but another door opened. “You’ll see this [in people who play] string instruments and piano. A lot of us tend to gravitate towards the math and sciences,” noted Giuliano. During her graduate studies at Tufts University, Giuliano became interested in pathology. When she expressed her enthusiasm in the field to Martha Hutchinson , who headed the pathology department at Tufts University at that time, Hutchinson offered her a piece of advice that shaped Giuliano’s career path. “[Hutchinson] said, ‘This group from Germany has identified this virus that they think is the cause of cervical cancer. So, I want you to learn everything that you can about it’,” recalled Giuliano. This virus was HPV, which virologist Harald zur Hausen and his colleagues had found in cervical cancer samples. Scientists also found that DNA from HPV-16, the HPV type most commonly found in cervical cancer cells, could induce cancer-like traits in cultured cells, validating that HPV infections could cause cervical cancer. 4 Given this compelling evidence and Hutchinson’s nudge, Giuliano knew what she wanted to do after finishing her graduate studies in 1989. “I'm going to prevent cervical cancer,” Giuliano declared back then. She chose to pursue a fellowship at the University of Arizona, where she could be close to the US-Mexico border, an area that had one of the highest rates of cervical cancer. 5 Chasing a Better Understanding of HPV Infections and Cancers At the University of Arizona, Giuliano crossed paths with gynecological oncologists Kenneth Hatch and Achim Schneider . Hatch was interested in learning more about nutrition in cervical cancer, and Schneider had trained under zur Hausen, who eventually went on to win the Nobel Prize for his discovery that HPV causes cervical cancer. A common goal united Giuliano, Hatch, and Schneider: They wanted to better understand HPV infections and cervical cancer . “It was a trifecta,” recalled Giuliano. “It was Ken as a physician, Achim, who set up the first HPV assays, and me as a burgeoning epidemiologist.” However, the trio had to fight through meager funding, which was difficult to come by since cervical cancer incidence was low in the US. “We spent a lot of time writing grants and then revising and resubmitting and so on,” said Giuliano. “A lot of that time could have just been done spent working on the research.” Despite this, they persevered and uncovered important insights about HPV infections and cervical cancer. One of their first findings was that people with recurrent HPV infections had lower antioxidant nutrients levels in their plasma. This helped establish that nutrient cofactors played a role in HPV infection risk. 6 Beyond nutritional studies, Giuliano and her team’s epidemiological studies helped elucidate the rate at which HPV infections are acquired and cleared. 7 Over time, she went on to investigate HPV in multicultural populations, realizing her dream of helping people from diverse backgrounds. At the turn of the century, scientists recognized that people from minority populations were at risk of acquiring HPV infections due to poor diet, early age of first intercourse, and multiple sexual partners. 8 However, few epidemiological studies included minority populations in the US, impeding scientists from getting a complete picture of HPV incidence among people from these backgrounds. 9 Giuliano and her team recruited participants belonging to Black and Hispanic populations and found that they had a higher HPV infection burden compared to people from majority populations. This offered significant evidence that certain groups would benefit more from vaccination efforts. 8,10 HPV Vaccine Testing in Women and Men In 1999, Giuliano received a phone call that proved to be pivotal. Eliav Barr , who was leading the clinical development program for the HPV vaccine at Merck, contacted Giuliano seeking a collaboration. He had come across one of her research abstracts and hoped her expertise would help him and his team conduct vaccine trials in healthy volunteers and follow them up over a long duration. “I said, ‘Yeah this is wonderful. I'm so excited to be part of the program’,” Giuliano recalled. The duo initially tested a monovalent vaccine—against one HPV antigen—followed by studies involving multivalent vaccines. 11,12 This culminated in a broad-spectrum FDA-approved vaccine that protects against nine HPV strains that cause nearly 90 percent of all cervical cancers. 13 As the president of the International Papillomavirus Society (IPVS), Giuliano presided over the final comments at the IPVS 2025 conference held in Bangkok. Anna Giuliano However, vaccinating women solved only half the problem. Studies in men revealed that they exhibited a higher prevalence of HPV infections compared to women. 14 Through her own research, Guiliano also had a good understanding of the natural history of HPV infection and screening strategies in men. 15 Since men could transmit HPV to their female sexual partners to potentially cause cervical cancer, Giuliano championed for the need to vaccinate men to protect both sexes against the virus. 16 So, over time, Giuliano and Barr expanded their studies to include men and found that a multivalent vaccine protected them from HPV infection and its associated complications. 17 Giuliano believes that her work on understanding HPV mechanism and investigating HPV vaccine efficacy in men has been her most impactful and significant contribution to the field. Noel Brewer , a public health researcher at the University of North Carolina, who has met Giuliano at several conferences, agreed. “She's made really important contributions to our understanding of HPV in men,” he said. “She helped to move the US and other countries to approve the vaccine for men by establishing the epidemiology of HPV and associated disease in men and the impact of HPV vaccination on men's health.” Setting Sights on Eliminating Cervical Cancer When she moved to the Moffitt Cancer Center in 2004, Giuliano continued pursuing investigations related to cancer epidemiology among diverse populations. Her work offered a better understanding of HPV infections’ natural history, which expanded on the foundation laid by Pap smears for cervical screening. 18 For instance, she helped measure the burden of HPV infections in cancers other than that of the cervix to quantify the rate at which infection occurred and got cleared. 19,20 Parallelly, she continued working on improving HPV vaccinations and advocating the need to make the vaccines available. “[Giuliano] is one of the leading figures who developed the argument that cervical cancer could be eliminated,” noted Brewer. She championed for the elimination of HPV-related cancers and argued that this was feasible in countries that have resources for immunizations, screenings, and pre-cancer treatments. She also acted as a consultant to the WHO regarding HPV vaccination and research on cervical cancer. “[Giuliano’s] powerful framing of the epidemiological data led the WHO to establish a global initiative to eliminate cervical cancer.” Brewer noted that this helped increase the global reach of HPV vaccinations from 40 percent to roughly 90 percent of at-risk populations. “This will save millions of lives,” he added. In fact, Giuliano’s work continues to strengthen the three main pillars which are the basis of WHO’s target for eliminating cervical cancer: HPV vaccination, cervical screening, and precancer and cancer treatment. 18 HPV vaccine uptake significantly increased among both female and male populations in the US. Designed by Erin Lemieux; data adapted from World Health Organization Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination coverage . In part due to her efforts, along with those of others in the field, the rate of cervical cancer cases has dropped from 9.3 new cases per 100,000 people in 1990 to 7.8 new cases per 100,000 people in 2021 globally . The incidence also reduced in the US from 10.2 new cases per 100,000 people in 1990 to 6.5 new cases per 100,000 people in 2021. Maintaining a Legacy: Shaping Policies and Young Minds Over time, Giuliano’s drive became a lesson for those she mentored. Brittney Dickey , who joined Giuliano’s group as a postdoctoral researcher in 2020, recalled how Giuliano advised her to define her career by a long-term goal. Giuliano’s research extends to countries outside of the US. She participated in a three-day HPV workshop in Harare, Zimbabwe, focused on the basic science of HPV and associated diseases, and methods for their prevention, early detection, and treatment. Participants included people from Zimbabwe, Botswana, South Africa, and Zambia Anna Giuliano Towards the end of her postdoctoral fellowship, Dickey confided in Giuliano about her lack of motivation at the time. “She said, ‘You have to figure out what your passion is’,” recalled Dickey, now a public health researcher at University of Nebraska Medical Center. “And if you have that goal and you have something that you're working towards every day, it helps motivate you in those small projects.” Dickey observed this first-hand about Giuliano. “At some point along the way, she realized her passion was to eliminate HPV. It's very evident that that drives her as a scientist,” said Dickey. Indeed, Giuliano persisted against all odds and went on to work toward her dream, laying the foundation for efforts—including better screening and vaccinations—aimed at eliminating cervical cancer. Reflecting on her career, Giuliano said that one of the most exciting aspects has been seeing how well the vaccine works. “It is incredibly rare as a cancer researcher to develop a…product that has such great efficacy across the board across all males, females, different ages, different ethnicities, different world regions,” she said. “It's just been phenomenal. It's so hard to explain how wonderful that is.” Despite the success, she acknowledged that the problem is not completely solved yet. According to her, scientists, investors, governments, and other stakeholders must come together to develop sustainable programs for global dissemination of the vaccine. She hopes that in this manner, all people who are eligible receive the vaccine. “That would be my dream.” References Ferris DG, et al.
